# Stagnated Development of Home Language Vocabulary in Japanese–Chinese Bilingual Children at Risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder

## Abstract

Japanese–Chinese bilingual children are rapidly increasing in Japan. Recent research has suggested that bilingual children have a larger vocabulary in their environmental language than their home language. However, Japanese nursery teachers and public therapists have not focused on the children’s home language development. Moreover, using monolingual screening tests for bilingual children leads to under-diagnosing language delays and developmental problems. Nevertheless, only a few Japanese assessment instruments are translated into or from Chinese. We utilized bilingual assessment tools and investigated developmental concerns and language development in 92 Japanese–Chinese bilingual preschoolers aged 1–6 years at risk for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We found that typically developing children demonstrate increased vocabulary acquisition in both languages by age four. In contrast, children at risk for ASD exhibited gradual vocabulary growth in Japanese but showed no significant development in Chinese comprehensive or productive vocabulary after 30 months of age. Moreover, logistic regression analysis indicated a heightened risk of underdiagnosis among bilingual children with ASD when home language criteria were not considered. These findings underscore the need to employ bilingual screening tools for early identification, particularly around 2.5 years of age, to prevent overlooking delays in bilingual language development.

## Résumé

L'augmentation rapide des enfants bilingues japonais-chinois au Japon pose des défis diagnostiques, notamment parce que les tests de dépistage monolingues conduisent au sous-diagnostic des retards de langage. De plus, les professionnels se concentrent peu sur le développement de la langue minoritaire de ces enfants. Cette étude a utilisé des outils d'évaluation bilingues pour examiner le développement du langage chez 92 enfants d'âge préscolaire bilingues à risque de trouble du spectre autistique (TSA). Nous avons constaté que les enfants au développement typique présentent une acquisition de vocabulaire accrue dans les deux langues dès l'âge de quatre ans. En revanche, les enfants à risque de TSA ont montré une croissance progressive de leur vocabulaire japonais, mais aucun développement significatif de leur vocabulaire chinois réceptif ou expressif après 30 mois. L'analyse a également révélé un risque accru de sous-diagnostic de TSA lorsque les critères de la langue parlée à la maison n'étaient pas considérés. Ces résultats soulignent l'impératif d'utiliser des outils de dépistage bilingues pour une identification précoce, en particulier vers l'âge de deux ans et demi, afin de mieux identifier les retards spécifiques dans le développement linguistique bilingue.

## Resumen

El número de niños bilingües japonés-chino está aumentando rápidamente en Japón. Investigaciones recientes han demostrado que los niños bilingües tienen un vocabulario más amplio en el idioma de su entorno que en el idioma que hablan en casa. Sin embargo, los maestros de guardería y los terapeutas públicos japoneses no se han centrado en el desarrollo del idioma que hablan los niños en casa. Además, el uso de pruebas de detección monolingües para niños bilingües conduce a un infradiagnóstico de los retrasos en el lenguaje y los problemas de desarrollo. No obstante, solo unos pocos instrumentos de evaluación japoneses se han traducido al chino o del chino. Utilizamos herramientas de evaluación bilingües e investigamos los problemas de desarrollo y el desarrollo del lenguaje en 92 niños en edad preescolar bilingües japonés-chino de entre 1 y 6 años con riesgo de trastorno del espectro autista (TEA). Descubrimos que los niños con un desarrollo típico muestran una mayor adquisición de vocabulario en ambos idiomas a los cuatro años. Por el contrario, los niños con riesgo de TEA mostraron un crecimiento gradual del vocabulario en japonés, pero no mostraron un desarrollo significativo en chino después de los 30 meses. Además, el análisis de regresión logística indicó un mayor riesgo de infradiagnóstico entre los niños bilingües con TEA cuando no se tenían en cuenta los criterios del idioma que se habla en casa. Estos hallazgos subrayan la necesidad de emplear herramientas de detección bilingües para la identificación temprana, especialmente alrededor de los 2,5 años de edad, a fin de evitar pasar por alto los retrasos en el desarrollo del lenguaje bilingüe.

## Introduction

Japan is often regarded as a geographically isolated nation with a monolingual population, as more than 90% of its inhabitants speak Japanese. This linguistic homogeneity has shaped an education system that predominantly teaches in Japanese. However, a recent national survey indicates that approximately 115,000 Japanese public-school students are raised in multilingual environments, with nearly 60% of these students requiring Japanese language instructions. According to the same survey, the number of students needing Japanese language support has increased annually by approximately 10,000 (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology \[MEXT\], [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR8)).

Many bilingual or multilingual children in Japan struggle to receive the developmental or learning support they need, leading to gaps in their educational and developmental outcomes (Kanno & Varghese, [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR18)). Wiefferink et al. ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR17)) reported that bilingual children are likelier than monolingual ones to experience such difficulties. Moreover, bilingual children are less likely to receive social support. Moreover, parents of multilingual children were more likely to be concerned about their children’s language development than those of monolingual children (Grasso et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR4)). This situation is further complicated for non-Japanese parents and their children with developmental concerns, such as language delays or autism spectrum disorders (ASD) because early identification and intervention for non-Japanese-speaking families are often limited (Suzuki et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14); Fujigo et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR3)). Timely identification of potential developmental issues is essential for these bilingual children, as delays can exacerbate language imbalances and social difficulties. Thus, finding these students earlier would be necessary to deliver effective learning support.

However, therapists in Japan rarely have access to appropriate tools for screening bilingual children. In practice, these professionals administer Japanese-language screening tests to bilingual children. Recent studies have shown that using monolingual screening tests for bilingual children results in underdiagnosing language delays (Altman et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR1)). Altman and colleagues recruited bilingual Hebrew-speaking children who also spoke English or Russian as their first language and divided them into two groups using background data: bilinguals typically developing (TD) or bilingual language-delayed children. These children were assessed for language proficiency in their first and second languages, including expressive vocabulary, comprehensive vocabulary, and word-sentence structure, using first-language screening test only or both first-language and Hebrew screening tests. The results show that using monolingual tests with monolingual criteria for bilingual children resulted in lower diagnostic accuracy, whereas using bilingual criteria for bilingual children resulted in higher diagnostic accuracy. Another study (Verbeek et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)) shows that bilingual three-to-five-year-old children with developmental disabilities exhibit smaller vocabulary sizes in their first and second languages than bilingual TD children and monolingual children with or without developmental disabilities. Interestingly, Verbeek et al. showed that bilingual children with developmental disabilities had a smaller vocabulary size in their first (home) language than in their second (environmental) language. Moreover, Grasso et al. ([2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR4)) indicated that bilingual children’s parents often refuse to speak their first language. These studies indicate the difficulty of identifying bilingual children at risk for ASD through first or second-language-based assessments only. Therefore, with bilingual children in Japan, it is necessary to use Japanese assessments and assessments translated into the second language or assessments translated into Japanese from the second language. Moreover, previous studies (Altman et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR1); Grasso et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR4); Verbeek et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)) mainly focused on language development at specific ages. However, there is little research on how bilingual children develop both languages as they age.

Although the significance of using multilingual assessments has been emphasized, Japanese teachers and public health nurses seldom attend to bilingual children’s home language development, focusing instead on their Japanese language acquisition (Suzuki et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14); Fujigo et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR3)). These professionals prioritize communication in Japanese with the children and their parents when assessing bilingual children, often failing to discern whether behavioral challenges arise from developmental concerns or cultural differences, particularly in the absence of formal language support systems. Rather than evaluating the children’s home language development, teachers and nurses frequently focus on the parents’ Japanese proficiency, relying on them to convey educational content to their children (Suzuki et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14); Fujigo et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR3)).

Suzuki et al. ([2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14)) reported that only 15 of 241 healthcare facilities used translated questionnaires for bilingual Asian children. Based on interview data, Fujigo et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR3)) similarly noted that nursery teachers prioritized play-based support for bilingual children while providing parents with assistance in interpretation and access to multilingual resources. Although such parental adaptation may support the child’s environmental language development, it can simultaneously hinder the development of the home language if that language is used infrequently (Montanari et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR9)). Therefore, Japanese teachers should be more careful in monitoring the frequency and quality of home language use in bilingual children.

According to MEXT ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR8)), the largest bilingual student group in Japan requiring language support are Chinese-speaking students, including Chinese and Taiwanese speakers. This group represents approximately 10% of children growing up in multilingual environments. Verbeek et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)) reported that bilingual children with developmental disabilities may struggle to transfer their home language skills to the environmental language. These findings highlight the significance of assessing the children’s Japanese language development and their home language abilities in identifying Japanese–Chinese bilingual children possibly at risk for developmental disabilities.

Researchers have often used the Japanese version of the MacArthur Communicative Development Inventories (J-CDI; Ogura, [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR10); Watamaki & Ogura, [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR16)). Ogura ([2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR10)) assessed the size of Japanese vocabulary. They have reported that typically developing Japanese children acquire more than 200 expressive vocabulary words by age two. Conversely, children at risk for ASD acquire only about 33 words at the same age (Okumura & Kobayashi, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR11)). In a similar study conducted in China, Su et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR12)) reported that four-year-old children with ASD and low verbal profiles produced an average of only 16.51 expressive words. However, their peers with high verbal profiles produced an average of 308.66 words. These findings suggest that Japanese–Chinese bilingual children with ASD have a similar developmental course.

Many studies have been conducted on English–Chinese bilingual children (e.g., Sun et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR13)), whereas research on Japanese–Chinese bilingual children’s vocabulary development is limited. Therefore, this study assessed the language development of Japanese–Chinese bilingual children typically developing and at risk for ASD. We selected a subset of vocabulary items from the J-CDI and translated them into Chinese. Moreover, it is also necessary to identify language delays and other developmental disabilities in Japanese–Chinese bilingual children using developmental assessment instruments. The commonly used instruments for evaluating developmental concerns used in Japan include the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT; Kamio et al., [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR6)) and the Parenting and Autism Research Scale—Text Revision (PARS-TR; Ito et al., [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR5)). These instruments are usually administered in Japanese. However, it is possible that Chinese translations would enhance the applicability of these instruments for bilingual children. According to Cohen et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR2)), relying solely on environmental language assessments can delay identifying developmental concerns, leading to underdiagnosis in bilingual populations. Therefore, we considered it crucial to evaluate children’s development using home language-based screening tools with Japanese translations.

The Taipei City Developmental Screening Checklist for Preschoolers, 2nd Version (Taipei-II; Liao et al., [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR7)) was used to address this need. This scale, which was developed in Taiwan, is designed to assess developmental milestones in several domains, including language, gross motor, fine motor, and socio-emotional development. This tool has official Japanese translations, making it suitable for Japanese–Chinese bilingual children. Many previous studies have assessed language development using multilingual vocabulary measures (e.g., Grasso et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR4); Sun et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR13); Verbeek et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)). The current study adds to the literature by evaluating developmental concerns using a Japanese screening tool translated into Chinese and a Chinese screening tool translated into Japanese.

This study conducted a cross-sectional analysis of language development and developmental concerns in 92 Japanese–Chinese bilingual preschoolers aged 1–6 years, with and without risk for ASD. Participants were categorized into two groups based on developmental concerns identified through clinical evaluations, national health checkups, or observations in nursery schools. To assess vocabulary development, we created a bilingual Japanese–Chinese checklist consisting of 301 words in each language, based in part on the Japanese Communicative Development Inventories (J-CDI). We hypothesized that TD Japanese–Chinese bilingual children would exhibit balanced language development in Japanese and Chinese, approaching the vocabulary sizes reported for monolingual children (Ogura, [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR10); Su et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR12)). In contrast, we expected that Japanese–Chinese bilingual children at risk for ASD would demonstrate reduced vocabulary development in their home language, because previous study has shown that bilingual children with developmental disabilities had a smaller vocabulary size in their home language than in their environmental language (Verbeek et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)).

We administered the M-CHAT and PARS-TR in Japanese with Chinese translation and the Taipei-II in Japanese to evaluate developmental concerns. A key objective was to determine whether the Japanese-translated version of the Taipei-II could effectively identify developmental concerns in bilingual children. We anticipated combining this tool with Japanese assessments translated into Chinese would improve diagnostic sensitivity and help mitigate the underdiagnosis of developmental concerns in bilingual populations (Cohen et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR2)).

## Methods

### Participants

We conducted a G power analysis to determine the required sample size. According to the analysis results, we needed a minimum of 14 participants to identify a partial *partial η*<sup><em>2</em></sup> of 0.20 or higher when using a three-way mixed factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) at *p* = 0.05 and a power of 98%. Therefore, 100 Japanese–Chinese bilingual children aged 1–6 years (mean age = 37.18 months) residing in Japan were recruited for the study. All the recruits had been bilingual for over 24 months. The sample comprised 56 children from Japanese–Chinese families (mean age = 36.91 months) and 44 from Chinese-Chinese families (mean age = 35.57 months). All of them were enrolled in mainstream classes of public or private nursery schools or kindergartens in Japan and used Japanese as the environmental language.

In the case of Japanese–Chinese families, 74.14% primarily used Japanese at home and Chinese as their second language. Regarding children from Chinese-Chinese families, 69.05% primarily used Chinese at home and Japanese as their second language. Moreover, 96% of mothers stated that they spoke Chinese as their home language and 40% of fathers spoke Chinese. The remaining parents primarily spoke Japanese at home.

Eight children from the Chinese-Chinese group were excluded from further analyses due to incomplete questionnaire responses. The final sample of 92 participants was divided into two groups based on prior identification of developmental concerns through clinical assessment, Japanese national health checkups, or reports from nursery schools. The group identified as being at risk for ASD consisted of 24 children (mean age = 41.04 months), whereas the TD group consisted of 68 children (mean age = 35.78 months). Children in the ASD risk group were those who had been identified as having concerns about ASD during Japanese national health checkups conducted at either with 18 months, 3 years, or 5 years of age and clinical screenings, whereas TD children were not having concerns.

We categorized the participants into three chronological age groups and examined developmental differences across these age groups. The younger group included 30 children under 24 months of age, consisting of 3 children in the ASD-at-risk group and 27 from the TD group. There were 32 children in the intermediate group (age 25 to 42 months), 12 in the ASD-at-risk group, and 20 in the TD group. The older group included 30 children (age 48 months or more); 9 were in the ASD-at-risk group and 21 from the TD group.

Waseda University Institutional Review Board approved this study (IRB; approval number: 2023 − 139). Following IRB approval, participants were recruited in Tokyo. Written and oral informed consent was obtained from all participants and their parents before data collection began.

### Instruments

The participants were assessed using four instruments: the Parent-Interview ASD Rating Scales—Text Revision (PARS-TR), the Taipei City Developmental Screening Checklist for Preschoolers, 2nd Version (Taipei-II; Liao et al., [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR7)), the Japanese/Chinese Vocabulary Checklist, and the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Japanese Version (M-CHAT). Before administering the assessments, the two authors discussed how to present the items appropriately to the parents, particularly for translation purposes.

The M-CHAT is a parent-report screening tool that consists of 23 yes/no questions. This scale is designed to detect ASD in children aged 16–30 months. A score of three or more failed items indicates a risk for ASD. We asked parents of children older than 25 months or younger than 18 months to recall their child’s behavior at the 18-month health checkup or to evaluate current behavior using the checklist. The first author translated the M-CHAT items into Chinese for Chinese-speaking parents.

The PARS-TR is a semi-structured interview used to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of ASD-related behaviors in children aged 36 months and older. Interviews were conducted in Chinese. The PARS-TR yields two scores: one reflecting current developmental concerns and another reflecting peak symptom severity. A score of nine or more failed items is considered the cutoff for ASD risk on the present and peak scales. We asked parents of children under 36 months to evaluate only their child’s current behaviors.

The Taipei-II is a parent-report checklist comprising 13 yes/no questions to detect developmental and language-related concerns in young children. This instrument, available in Chinese and Japanese, is structured as an age-specific checklist for children aged 3–60 months. In this study, both the Japanese and Chinese versions of Taipei-II were administered, and failure to meet the screening criteria was defined as failing the assessment in both languages.

The Japanese–Chinese Vocabulary Checklist is a 602-item parent-report questionnaire designed to assess language development in Japanese–Chinese bilingual children. This tool was adapted from the Japanese MacArthur Communicative Development Inventory (J-CDI) for children aged 16–36 months. We selected 301 Japanese noun words from the J-CDI and translated them into Chinese. Parents were asked to record their child’s vocabulary by indicating whether each word was understood (receptive) or understood and spoken (productive) in each language over one week. The parents of children aged 37 months or older were instructed to evaluate their child’s language abilities based on their current status.

### Procedure

Participants’ parents were asked to complete the vocabulary checklist before participating in the developmental interviews. The interviews were conducted individually in a laboratory at Waseda University in the Tokyo region. The first author conducted the Parent-Interview ASD Rating Scales—Text Revision (PARS-TR) interviews with each parent, using Chinese and Japanese as appropriate for the respondent’s language preference. Following the PARS-TR interview, parents were asked to complete the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT), which was provided with both oral and written Chinese translations. The Japanese and Chinese versions of Taipei-II were jointly administered by the first author and the parents.

### Dependent Variables and Data Analysis

The dependent variables in this study included several key developmental and language measures. Firstly, we examined the mean scores on the PARS-TR, which reflected parental reports of the child’s developmental concerns at present and peak times. A score exceeding nine was considered indicative of ASD risk. Secondly, we analyzed the mean scores on the M-CHAT, where the number of failed items was recorded. A score greater than three indicated a potential developmental concern. Thirdly, based on parent responses, we assessed the mean scores on the Taipei-II. A cutoff score above two was used to indicate developmental risk. In addition to these screening scores, we measured the mean number of comprehensive vocabulary items in Japanese and Chinese, defined as the number of words the child was reported to understand. We also measured the mean number of productive vocabulary items in both languages, which was defined as the number of words the child was reported to understand and speak correctly.

We conducted mixed factorial analyses of variance (ANOVAs) on the developmental scores of all 92 participants. The primary ANOVA design consisted of a 2 (Group: TD vs. ASD-at-risk; between-subjects) × 3 (Chronological Age: younger, intermediate, and older; between-subjects) factorial structure to examine group and age-related differences in developmental measures. To further investigate language development, we conducted additional mixed ANOVAs with a 2 (Group: TD vs. ASD-at-risk; between-subjects) × 3 (Chronological Age: younger, intermediate, and older; between-subjects) × 2 (Language: Japanese vs. Chinese; within-subjects) design. These analyses focused on the number of comprehensive and productive vocabulary items to assess bilingual language development patterns across groups and age categories. When appropriate, we performed Post hoc analyses using Bonferroni’s multiple comparison tests to clarify significant interaction effects. Finally, we conducted binary logistic regression analyses to determine whether developmental screening scores and vocabulary development could predict ASD risk across participants of all ages. We created dummy variables for each screening measure in the regression analysis. Children scoring above nine on the PARS-TR peak score were coded as 1 (indicating ASD risk) and others as 0. Similarly, we coded children scoring above nine on the PARS-TR present score, such that those scoring above three on the M-CHAT were coded as 1, and those scoring above two on the Taipei-II were also coded as 1. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to evaluate the predictive strength of each variable in identifying children at risk for ASD.

### Vocabulary Development

![Figure 1](https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs13158-025-00473-x/MediaObjects/13158_2025_473_Fig1_HTML.png)

**Figure 1.**

Comprehensive and productive vocabulary development for all participants

Figure [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Fig1) illustrates the two types of vocabulary development observed in all the participants. Figure [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Fig1)a shows the mean comprehensive vocabulary size. The bilingual TD children increased their Japanese vocabulary from 71.81 (SE = 13.92) to 249.55 (SE = 17.07) and then to 275.14 (SE = 16.84) words, respectively, in younger, intermediate and older groups. Younger, intermediate, and older children also increased their comprehensive Chinese vocabulary, respectively, from 102.59 (SE = 15.78) to 246.00 (SE = 18.04) and then to 277.48 (SE = 17.03) words. Moreover, younger, intermediate, and older ASD-at-risk children increased their Japanese vocabulary respectively from 52.33 (SE = 24.55) to 152.58 (SE = 24.32) and then to 254.00 (SE = 22.58) words and their Chinese comprehensive vocabularies increased from 33.67 (SE = 14.34) to 184.33 (SE = 29.41), and then to 183.89 (SE = 34.37) words.

We observed a significant three-way interaction among the group, age, and language, *F* (2, 86) = 3.36, *p* = 0.039, *partial η²* = 0.072. Post hoc analyses indicated significant simple-simple main effects between the intermediate age groups for Japanese, *F* (1, 86) = 18.42, *p* = 0.000, *partial η²* = 0.176, and Chinese vocabulary *F* (1, 86) = 4.58, *p* = 0.035, *partial η²* = 0.051. The older groups only showed differences in Chinese vocabulary development, *F* (1, 86) = 8.88, *p* = 0.004, *partial η²* = 0.094. We also found significant simple-simple main effects of language development for younger age in the TD group, *F* (1, 86) = 4.03, *p* = 0.048, *partial η²* = 0.045, and for older age in the ASD-at-risk group, *F* (1, 86) = 6.97, *p* = 0.010, *partial η²* = 0.075. Additionally, both groups displayed other simple, main effects of age on language development.

These findings indicated that the TD groups increased their comprehensive vocabulary from younger to intermediate age, which reached a ceiling in the older age for Japanese, *F* (2, 86) = 78.31, *p* = 0.000, *partial η²* = 0.646, and Chinese, *F* (2, 86) = 34.15, *p* = 0.000, *partial η²* = 0.443. Children in the ASD-at-risk group gradually developed their Japanese comprehensive vocabulary from younger to older, *F* (2, 86) = 13.99, *p* = 0.000, *partial η²* = 0.245. However, their Chinese comprehensive vocabulary did not increase from intermediate to older age, although it increased from younger to intermediate age, *F* (2, 86) = 4.78, *p* = 0.011, *partial η²* = 0.100. These findings suggested that younger bilingual TD children had a larger comprehensive Chinese than a Japanese vocabulary. In contrast, younger ASD-at-risk children displayed comparable vocabulary development across the two languages. Conversely, older bilingual TD children had a comparable vocabulary in both languages, whereas older ASD-at-risk children had a larger Japanese vocabulary than Chinese. We also found that TD children in the intermediate age group had a larger comprehensive Japanese and Chinese vocabulary than those with age-matched ASD-at-risk children.

Figure [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Fig1)b displays the mean number of productive vocabulary items. The younger, intermediate, and older children in the bilingual TD group increased their Japanese productive vocabulary, respectively, from 26.04 (SE = 7.76) to 204.05 (SE = 9.75) and then to 260.10 (SE = 9.69) words. Moreover, younger, intermediate, and older children’s Chinese productive vocabulary increased, respectively, from 51.33 (SE = 12.33) to 192.15 (SE = 14.18) and then to 256.95 (SE = 13.80) words. In contrast, younger, intermediate, and older children in the ASD-at-risk group increased their Japanese productive vocabulary, respectively from 16.67 (SE = 8.09) to 84.08 (SE = 28.29) words and eventually to 220.22 (SE = 32.94) words. Moreover, younger and intermediate children’s Chinese productive vocabulary grew, respectively, from 9.33 (SE = 2.96) to 114.42 (SE = 35.10) words but then increased only modestly to 144.67 (SE = 40.39) words in older children.

A significant three-way interaction was again observed among group, age, and language, *F*(2, 86) = 3.12, *p* = 0.049, *partial η²* = 0.068. Post hoc analyses revealed significant simple-simple main effects in the intermediate age group for Japanese, *F*(1, 86) = 25.63, *p* < 0.001, *partial η²* = 0.230, and Chinese vocabulary, *F*(1, 86) = 5.88, *p* = 0.017, *partial η²* = 0.064, between TD and ASD-at-risk children. A significant difference was again observed in the older group for Chinese productive vocabulary, *F*(1, 86) = 10.31, *p* = 0.002, *partial η²* = 0.107. Moreover, we also observed a significant language difference within the older ASD-at-risk group, *F*(1, 86) = 6.94, *p* = 0.010, *partial η²* = 0.075.

We also conducted additional age-related analyses. These analyses indicated that TD children’s productive vocabulary steadily increased from the younger to the older group in Japanese, *F*(2, 86) = 86.39, *p* < 0.001, *partial η²* = 0.668 and reached a peak for Chinese in the intermediate group, *F*(2, 86) = 34.79, *p* < 0.001, *partial η²* = 0.447. On the other hand, children at risk for ASD did not show significant productive vocabulary growth until after age four, *F*(2, 86) = 16.24, *p* < 0.001, *partial η²* = 0.274. Moreover, their Chinese productive vocabulary was relatively stable across age groups, *F*(2, 86) = 2.68, *p* = 0.074, *partial η²* = 0.059.

These results suggest that older bilingual TD children developed productive vocabulary in both languages equally, whereas older children at risk for ASD exhibited significantly more productive vocabulary in Japanese than in Chinese. Also, TD children in the intermediate age group had significantly larger productive vocabularies in both Japanese and Chinese than their age-matched peers at risk for ASD.

### Binary Logistic Regression Analyses for Indicating ASD-at-Risk

**Table 2.** Binary logistic regression for the probability of indicating ASD-at-risk

| Variables                             | β     | SE                         | Wald  | *p*     | OR     | 95% CI for Exp / Lower | 95% CI for Exp / Upper | 95% CI for Exp / Upper |
| ------------------------------------- | ----- | -------------------------- | ----- | ------- | ------ | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Chronological age                     | 0.06  | 0.04                       | 2.23  | 0.135   | 1.06   | 0.98                   | 0.98                   | 1.14                   |
| Taipei-II cutoff                      | 5.30  | 1.07                       | 24.71 | 0.000\* | 199.53 | 24.73                  | 24.73                  | 1610.05                |
| Chinese productive<br>vocabulary size | -0.01 | 0.01 | 3.88 | 0.049\* | 0.99 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 1.00 |
| Intercept | -3.61 | 0.25<sup>a</sup><br>(0.06) | 7.91 | 0.005 | 0.03 | | | |

Correctly classified: 93.5%, *R*<sup><em>2</em></sup> Nagelkerke = 0.75

We conducted a binary logistic regression analysis using the likelihood ratio method to identify variables that significantly predicted ASD risk. Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Tab2) presents the results of the model, which demonstrated a statistically significant fit, *p* < 0.001. The Hosmer and Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test indicated an adequate model fit, *p* = 0.553, and the model correctly classified 93.5% of cases. The Nagelkerke *R²* value was 0.75, suggesting a strong explanatory capacity.

Chronological age did not affect the models significantly. However, the odds ratio (OR) for the Taipei-II cutoff variable exceeded 1. This finding suggests that the likelihood of being classified as at risk for ASD increased by a factor of 199.53 for each unit increase above the Taipei-II cutoff score. Conversely, we observed OR values below one for Chinese productive vocabulary development, signifying that the probability of ASD-at-risk decreases by 0.99 times for each point, and the score in this variable decreased.

These findings suggest that bilingual children with ASD risk are more likely to be underdiagnosed when clinicians rely solely on environmental language assessments and overlook home language development, which is particularly the case for productive vocabulary in the home language. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating home language–based screening tools, such as the Taipei-II and bilingual vocabulary assessments, in early developmental evaluations for bilingual children.

## Discussion

This cross-sectional study examined language development and developmental concerns in 92 Japanese–Chinese bilingual preschoolers aged 1–6 years, with or without risk for ASD. As shown in Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Fig1), comprehensive and productive vocabulary sizes in Japanese and Chinese were comparable between TD children and those at risk for ASD before age two. However, TD children demonstrated a rapid increase in vocabulary size in both languages by the age of four, while children at risk for ASD showed only a gradual increase in Japanese vocabulary and no meaningful development in Chinese vocabulary after 30 months of age.

While previous research has primarily focused on specific age points between two and eight years or has relied on longitudinal designs (e.g., Su et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR12)), our study contributes new cross-sectional data across a broader developmental range. Our findings highlight that bilingual children at risk for ASD experience delays in comprehensive and productive language development across their home and environmental languages, particularly before age four.

Verbeek et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)) reported that bilingual children with developmental disabilities often struggle to transfer skills from their home language to the environmental language and tend to show similarly limited development in both languages. Our results partially replicate these findings by demonstrating that Japanese–Chinese bilingual children at risk for ASD gradually improve their Japanese vocabulary after age four. However, the ceiling effect in the Japanese vocabulary checklist used in this study may influence this apparent catch-up effect. Verbeek et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)) used a relatively limited vocabulary list of 64 words per language for children around age four. In contrast, Japanese studies have shown that TD children typically comprehend and produce around 200 words by the age of two (Ogura, [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR10); Okumura & Kobayashi, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR11)), and Chinese children reach approximately 310 words by 4.5 years of age (Su et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR12)).

In light of these developmental benchmarks and the structure of the Japanese Communicative Development Inventories (J-CDIs; Ogura, [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR10); Watamaki & Ogura, [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR16)), we expanded our checklist to include 301 nouns in both Japanese and Chinese. By age 3.5, TD bilingual children in our sample could comprehend and produce around 250 words in each language, with a modest increase to 275 words after age four. Children at risk for ASD reach 250 Japanese words after age four, suggesting that vocabulary development is on par with that of their TD peers in Japanese. However, since our checklist included only noun items, it may have limited our ability to detect further developmental differences. To more accurately assess whether bilingual children at risk for ASD can fully catch up to their TD peers, future research should expand the checklist to include verbs, adjectives, and other word classes.

Our participants at risk for ASD showed an increase in Chinese vocabulary size from 33 to 185 words by approximately 2.5 years of age. However, after this point, they exhibited no significant gains in comprehensive or productive Chinese vocabulary. Su and colleagues ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR12)) reported that monolingual children with ASD of low verbal proficiency increased their Chinese vocabulary size from 16 to 143 words as they grew from approximately 3.5 years to 4.5 years of age, but age-matched participants increased their vocabulary size from 308 to 470 words at the same timeline. Unlike monolingual children, our bilingual participants did not improve their vocabulary size after 2.5 years old, and these results might be due to the use of bilingual families in the home language. This stagnation may be attributed to patterns of home language use in bilingual families.

Previous studies have shown that bilingual children with developmental disabilities and their parents often avoid using the home language, instead prioritizing the environmental language due to challenges in comprehension and production (Grasso et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR4); Montanari et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR9)). Although 90% of mothers and 40% of fathers in our sample reported speaking Chinese at home, it is possible that children still struggled to process or respond to Chinese input effectively, leading to poor productive outcomes. These findings align with Verbeek et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)), who noted that children with ASD-at-risk face difficulties in leveraging home language skills to support environmental language development. Although children at risk for ASD in this study could not understand and produce their home language, tracking their home language development is essential for identifying developmental and language support needs in bilingual populations. Home language development provides a more comprehensive understanding of children’s linguistic profile and may help prevent misdiagnosis or oversight.

Using multilingual assessment tools avoids underdiagnosis in bilingual children (Altman et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR1); Cohen et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR2); Grasso et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR4)). According to Cohen et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR2)), monolingual assessment reduces intervention opportunities and early diagnosis for bilingual children. Therefore, we used the Japanese versions of the M-CHAT and PARS-TR, supplemented with oral and written Chinese translations with a Japanese translation of the Taipei-II, initially developed in Chinese.

Altman et al. ([2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR1)) demonstrated that using monolingual screening tools with monolingual criteria yields lower diagnostic accuracy, whereas bilingual criteria improve assessment outcomes. Accordingly, we adopted both monolingual and bilingual criteria in our study. As reflected in the results (Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Tab1)), bilingual children at risk for ASD could be identified using the M-CHAT with Chinese oral translation in younger age groups and the PARS-TR for older children. The Taipei-II, administered in both Japanese and Chinese but based initially on Chinese developmental criteria, also successfully detected developmental concerns in children older than 2.5 years.

These findings suggest that screening tools incorporating bilingual criteria—either through translation or adaptation—are particularly effective in identifying children at risk for ASD around 2.5 years of age. While Japanese-translated monolingual assessments may still be helpful after age four, reliance on them alone may lead to underdiagnosis. Integrating bilingual approaches early on is essential for accurate identification and support.

We also conducted a binary logistic regression analysis using the likelihood ratio method to identify predictors of ASD risk among bilingual children. As shown in Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#Tab2), bilingual children at risk for ASD were most accurately identified by two variables: whether they exceeded the cutoff score on the Taipei-II and their Chinese productive vocabulary size across ages. These results suggest that relying solely on Japanese screening tools and vocabulary assessments may be insufficient for identifying bilingual children at risk for ASD.

In Japan, this challenge is compounded by limited access to translated assessment tools. Suzuki et al. ([2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14)) reported that only 6.22% of healthcare facilities had implemented translated questionnaires for bilingual Asian children. As a result, early identification, intervention, and educational support for children from non-Japanese-speaking families are often inadequate (Kanno & Varghese, [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR18); Suzuki et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14); Fujigo et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR3)). Fujigo et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR3)) further noted that nursery teachers tended to focus more on parents’ use of Japanese than on the child’s home language development, suggesting a systemic lack of awareness about the linguistic needs of bilingual children.

If applying fully translated Japanese screening tools proves problematic in practice, it may still be beneficial for educators, healthcare providers, and caregivers to track the number of productive words a child can use in their home language. Based on our findings, children who comprehended fewer than 150 Japanese and 180 Chinese words or who produced fewer than 85 Japanese and 115 Chinese words around the age of three may exhibit traits associated with ASD. Furthermore, our results suggest that bilingual children at risk for ASD typically do not experience further growth in home language vocabulary after 4 years of age. Therefore, clinicians and educators should pay attention to a child’s language development and adaptive behavior in the environmental language and their progress in the home language.

This study has several limitations that should be addressed in future research. Firstly, future studies should include monolingual Japanese and monolingual Chinese participants to isolate bilingual-specific developmental patterns better. Verbeek et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR15)) included monolingual speakers of the environmental language. However, they did not include monolingual home language users. Comparative analyses among monolingual Japanese, Chinese, and bilingual children are expected to provide a more comprehensive understanding of language development in different linguistic contexts.

Secondly, our vocabulary checklist was limited to nouns. Su and colleagues ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR12)) reported that monolingual children with ASD of low verbal proficiency increased their Chinese vocabulary size from 16 to 143 words as they grew from about 3.5 years to 4.5 years of age. However, age-matched participants with high verbal fluency increased their vocabulary size from 308 to 470 words during the same period. Unlike monolingual children, the bilingual participants did not improve their vocabulary size after 2.5 years of age, which might be due to the home language use of bilingual families.

Finally, there is a need to develop comprehensive screening tools suitable for monolingual and bilingual children. Few public services in Japan are equipped to administer bilingual assessments (Suzuki et al., [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR14)). Relying on separate or additional screenings increases clinicians’ workload and response burden, particularly in public health settings. Therefore, a more efficient approach may involve the development of integrated screening tools that incorporate both monolingual and bilingual criteria. Alternatively, using translated versions of validated foreign screening tools, such as the Taipei-II, or non-verbal developmental assessments could offer viable solutions.

Early detection is essential for implementing effective interventions and providing adequate educational and social support. This study’s findings highlight the significant risks of overlooking bilingual children’s home language development. MEXT (2024) reports a continued increase in the number of multilingual students in Japan, a traditionally monolingual society. As a result, the need to expand developmental, educational, and social support for monolingual and bilingual children and their families is increasing, and it is crucial for reducing disparities in developmental outcomes (Kanno & Varghese, [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13158-025-00473-x#ref-CR18)).

## Conclusion

This cross-sectional study of Japanese–Chinese bilingual children (1–6 years) highlights critical differences in early language trajectories between typically developing (TD) children and those at risk for ASD, emphasizing the necessity of bilingual-sensitive assessment. In conclusion, early detection, which is crucial for effective intervention, requires comprehensive assessment that acknowledges and tracks the development of a bilingual children’s home language (Chinese) in addition to the environmental language (Japanese). Given the increasing number of multilingual students in Japan, expanding developmental and educational support that accounts for linguistic diversity is essential for reducing uneven language development.
